description: The reconnect-resume shim: the document-start script the iOS client installs so the Control UI's chat page can send after a reconnect while the gateway still refuses the marker the page puts on that frame. This file is the ONE owner of the reserved property name, the method it travels on, and the injected script itself; core/reconnect-resume-shim.js reads it, core/test/reconnect-resume-shim.test.js drives the script against a fake window and WebSocket, and the iOS client bundles THIS FILE and installs the script through a WKUserScript, so there is one copy of the script in the tree rather than one per client. The desktop needs no shim, because the gateway's own strip covers the browser Control UI connection.
why: The marker, and why the page sets it. The Control UI marks the first chat.send after a reconnect so the gateway resumes the conversation rather than reading the send as a new message: requestChatSend in the OpenClaw checkout at ui/src/pages/chat/chat-send-request.ts puts `__controlUiReconnectResume: true` on that frame's params, and clears its own record of the resumed session only AFTER the send succeeds.

The gateway strips that marker, but only for some clients. resolveControlUiReconnectResumeParams in the checkout at src/gateway/server-methods/chat-server-timing.ts removes the field from the params it validates ONLY when the calling client is one the server counts as an operator UI, and that predicate (isOperatorUiClient in src/utils/message-channel.ts) matches the browser-side ids alone: control-ui, browser-copilot and tui. For every other client the params come back untouched, the still-present field then fails chat.send's own parameter validation, and the WHOLE send is refused with `invalid chat.send params: at root: unexpected property '__controlUiReconnectResume'`.

Why the phone is the client that hits this. This app's page connects with a NATIVE descriptor rather than a browser one (id openclaw-ios, mode ui, built by mobile/Chela/NativeControlAuth.swift), which is not among the ids that strip is gated on, so the marker is never removed for this client and every resumed send is refused.

Why the failure outlives the one send. Because the page clears its resume record only on a successful send, a single refusal leaves the marker on the frame it builds next: every later chat.send carries it, every one is refused the same way, and only relaunching the app clears it. The reader sees `Not sent · Retry` on a message that will never send, over a connection that is otherwise healthy, which is the worst shape this can take: the surface says nothing about why.

Why a shim here rather than the fix, and why not a different client id. The durable fix is upstream and is filed separately: the gateway should strip this reserved field for EVERY client, whatever connect descriptor it used, because the field is the page's own and no client should have to be on a list for the gateway to understand it. This shim is the prevention, so the phone works before that ships, and it lives in the client because nothing else on this side can reach the frame: the field is written by the page onto the socket it owns, so the last place it can be dropped before the gateway refuses it is that socket. Adopting a browser client id to pass the gate is deliberately not the shape of this: it would make this client claim to be a different one, and the gateway's own logs would stop telling the phone from a browser on the same device, which is the reason the native descriptor exists at all.

Why document start. The wrapper has to be in place before the page's own script captures or calls `WebSocket.prototype.send`, the same timing and the same reason as the client-context hook and the pairing observer: a wrapper added at document end would be racing a socket the page had already opened, and the frames it missed would be silent. It takes the method as it stands at install time and calls it through, so a second wrapper on the same method, which the client-context hook is, composes with this one in either order.

Why every other frame is left alone. A frame is rewritten only when it is a request, its method is chat.send, and its params object actually carries the reserved property. Everything else is handed to the original send as the exact string it arrived as, and the whole wrapper sits inside a try/catch that falls through to the original call: this script runs in a page we do not own, and a wrapper that threw or rewrote something it did not recognise would break far more than the one send it exists to fix. The VALUE is not the test, because the property itself is what the gateway refuses: the page only ever sets it true, and a false one would fail the same validation, so it is deleted too rather than left to fail the send.

THE REMOVAL TRIGGER: delete this shim once the released gateway strips the reserved field for every client, whatever the connect descriptor says, because that is the exact condition the shim stands in for. At that point the marker never reaches chat.send's validation on any client, and this is one more wrapper on the page's socket earning nothing. What retires it is a gateway release carrying the upstream fix, not a date and not our own build. Its removal is a file deletion plus every pointer: core/spec/reconnect-resume-shim.json, core/reconnect-resume-shim.js and its test, the app's resource entry in mobile/project.yml, the WKUserScript registration in mobile/Chela/WebView.swift, and the parity test beside it.
hook: // A page with no socket constructor has nothing to wrap, and a wrapper over
// nothing would throw where the page expected to work. The guard mirrors the
// pairing observer's, which returns on a missing socket for the same reason.
// The property itself is what the gateway refuses, never its value: the page
// only ever sets it true, and a false one would fail the same validation, so
// the test is presence rather than truthiness.
// The exact envelope the page sends, and nothing else: a request, the
// chat.send method, and the reserved property on a params object. Anything
// this does not recognise goes out as the same bytes it came in as.
try { frame = JSON.parse(data); } catch (error) { return data; }
if (!frame || frame.type !== 'req' || frame.method !== METHOD || !carriesReserved(frame.params)) return data;
